title: The Office Company That Burned $47 Billion
hook: In January 2019, WeWork was valued at forty-seven billion dollars -- and it didn't own a single building it worked out of. Six weeks after filing to go public, that number was simply gone.
body:
WeWork was founded in 2010 by Adam Neumann and Miguel McKelvey, who had previously run a small coworking space called GreenDesk in Brooklyn starting in 2008. The first WeWork location opened in Manhattan's SoHo, backed by $15 million from an early investor; Adam's wife Rebekah Neumann joined as a co-founder and chief brand officer. Valuation climbed from $1.4 billion to $10.5 billion between 2014 and 2016. In 2017, SoftBank's Masayoshi Son visited WeWork's New York headquarters for about 30 minutes and committed $4.4 billion through the SoftBank Vision Fund, after Neumann told him the 'crazy guy' wins a fight. In January 2019, a SoftBank-led round valued the company -- rebranded 'The We Company' -- at $47 billion. On August 14, 2019, the company filed its S-1 for an IPO, disclosing 2018 revenue of $1.82 billion against a net loss of $1.93 billion, and a first-half-2019 loss over $900 million on $1.54 billion of revenue. The filing revealed WeWork had paid $5.9 million to a Neumann-controlled entity for rights to the 'We' trademark (later returned), a dual-class share structure giving Neumann's stock 20 votes per share (later cut to 10), and an invented non-GAAP metric called 'Community Adjusted EBITDA.' Investor backlash collapsed the offering: guidance fell to roughly $10-12 billion, Neumann resigned as CEO on September 24, 2019, and the company withdrew its S-1 on September 30, 2019 -- a drop of roughly $38-40 billion from the January peak in about six weeks. SoftBank stepped in with a rescue package worth roughly $9.5 billion; Neumann's own exit package was reported at up to $1.7 billion (about $970 million for his shares, a $185 million consulting fee, and $500 million in credit against personal loans). On November 21, 2019, WeWork laid off 2,400 employees, about 19% of its workforce. In May 2020, SoftBank marked its WeWork stake down to $2.9 billion and Masayoshi Son told investors, 'We made a failure on investing in WeWork ... I was foolish' and, separately, 'I was wrong.' WeWork went public a second time via a SPAC merger with BowX Acquisition Corp (announced March 2021, ~$9 billion valuation), debuting on the NYSE on October 21, 2021. In August 2022, venture firm Andreessen Horowitz invested $350 million in Neumann's new startup, Flow, valuing it at $1 billion before launch. In August 2023, WeWork issued a 'going concern' warning, by then worth around $270 million. On November 6, 2023, WeWork and 517 affiliated entities filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in New Jersey, listing $18.6 billion in debt against $15 billion in assets; about 90% of lenders agreed to convert $3 billion of debt to equity. Neumann, backed by Flow, made a bid (reported around $500 million) to buy WeWork back in March 2024, then abandoned it that spring, calling the bankruptcy 'disappointing.' WeWork emerged from Chapter 11 as a private company on June 11, 2024, eliminating over $4 billion of debt. This is what SEC filings (the August 2019 S-1, Chapter 11 petitions), SoftBank's own earnings-call statements, and contemporaneous reporting (CNBC, TechCrunch, Fortune, PitchBook) say happened.
